name: Dermaplaning razor

lead: Dermaplaning is a form of mechanical exfoliation in which a single sharp blade is drawn lightly across the face to remove the top layer of dead skin cells and fine vellus hair, or peach fuzz. Home versions use small, single-blade facial razors, while professionals use a scalpel.
It is used to get a smoother skin surface, brighter look and more even makeup and skincare application.

paras: The blade, held at a shallow angle, shaves off the stratum corneum and vellus hair at skin level. The hair follicle is untouched, so hair regrows on its normal schedule, and exfoliation lets products absorb more easily.

Risks include nicks, irritation and breakouts, and it is not advised over active acne or inflamed skin. Hair does not grow back thicker or darker, but the effects last only a few weeks. No controlled trials were identified, and the evidence comes from clinic and aesthetics sources, though the mechanism is physically straightforward. Using a clean blade is advised to reduce infection risk.

lead: Dermaplaning is a form of mechanical exfoliation in which a single sharp blade is drawn at a shallow angle across the face to remove the outermost layer of dead skin cells and fine vellus hair, commonly called peach fuzz. Clinicians and aestheticians perform it with a sterile surgical-style blade, and consumer versions are small single-blade facial razors sold for home use, typically at around $10 to $20 [1].

Users and practitioners describe the purpose as a smoother, brighter-looking skin surface and a more even base for makeup and skincare products. Reported effects last on the order of weeks, since the skin and hair regrow [1].

Published evidence is limited. A 2011 systematic review of dermaplaning, topical oxygen and light therapy found that the data supporting these noninvasive facial rejuvenation methods were scarce and largely anecdotal [2]. Laboratory studies show that dermaplaning removes part of the stratum corneum and can alter how drugs permeate excised skin [3][4], and older surgical literature describes the use of dermatome-based dermaplaning for acne scarring [5][6]. No controlled trial of the home facial razor for cosmetic smoothing is known.

paras: Home dermaplaning razors are small blades with a protective guard or handle designed for use on the face, while professional dermaplaning is performed by dermatologists, plastic surgeons or licensed aestheticians with a sterile blade [1]. Accounts of the technique describe holding the skin taut and drawing the blade in light strokes at a shallow angle, usually of around 45 degrees [1]. The treatment is generally described as a cosmetic exfoliation, distinct from chemical peels and microdermabrasion because it uses a manual blade and removes vellus hair at the same time [1].

The blade scrapes away the stratum corneum, the dead outer layer of skin, together with fine hair cut at the skin surface [1]. Histological work on dermaplaned skin has shown removal of the stratum corneum and parts of the viable epidermis [3]. Because the blade cuts hair at the surface, descriptions of the technique state that follicles are not altered and vellus hair regrows in its original fine form after a few weeks [1].

A laboratory study found that four strokes of a dermaplaning device caused a significant drop in the skin's electrical resistance, indicating loss of barrier function of the stratum corneum, and increased 24-hour permeation of two model drugs through excised skin, although absorption varied between samples [3]. A separate in vitro study compared dermaplaning with sonophoresis, laser, microneedles and microdermabrasion as ways to enhance transdermal delivery of naloxone, finding that all of these techniques shortened lag time compared with untreated skin [4]. These studies concern drug delivery models and not cosmetic outcomes.

Dermaplaning appears in the medical literature from at least the 1970s. Papers from 1977 describe dermaplaning, including with an electrokeratome device, as part of operations to level and revise the acne-scarred face, often combined with excision or chemical peeling [5][6]. A 1977 plastic surgery paper noted that treatments for acne pitting were often disappointing and advised surgeons to promise patients little improvement [6]. A 1980 review listed dermaplaning among alternatives to excisional surgery for facial skin lesions [7].

According to an AI-generated encyclopedia summary, the technique entered mainstream skincare in the 2010s through social media and celebrity endorsement, with the hashtag reportedly reaching billions of views by 2024 [1]. That claim comes from an untrusted secondary source and was not independently verified.

The 2011 systematic review identified 42 peer-reviewed English-language manuscripts on dermaplaning, oxygen therapy and light therapy, and concluded that the scientific data supporting them were scarce, anecdotal and not well documented, even though the treatments had grown popular with patients and practitioners [2]. Reported benefits such as a smoother surface, immediate brightness and easier makeup application rest mainly on practitioner and aesthetics-industry accounts [1]. The immediate removal of hair and surface scale is a direct physical effect of the blade, but its duration and any longer-term skin-quality effects have not been measured in published trials.
A 2011 systematic review in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery screened dermaplaning, topical oxygen and photodynamic therapy literature and found the evidence scarce and anecdotal [2].

Historical surgical papers from 1977 describe dermaplaning as one step in managing acne scarring and sycosis nuchae, using dermatomes rather than consumer razors [5][6][8]. A 2013 case report mentions dermaplaning and dermabrasion among techniques for rhinophyma [9].
No randomized controlled trial of home facial dermaplaning razors for skin appearance has been found.

Reported risks include nicks and cuts, temporary redness, irritation and breakouts, and increased sun sensitivity afterwards, with sunscreen commonly recommended by practitioners [1]. Descriptions of the procedure say it is not generally advised over active acne, eczema or inflamed skin, or soon after isotretinoin use [1]. Using unclean blades is associated with infection risk [1]. Some sources report that dermaplaning does not cause hair to grow back thicker or darker [1].

Dermaplaning is discussed as a low-cost step for smoother-looking skin and makeup application. Forum material specific to this entry was not available, so this article does not characterise community opinion.

Home dermaplaning razors are typically sold in multi-packs with replaceable blades at about $10 to $20. Features that vary include blade guard design, handle length and whether blades are single-use or replaceable.
